articles.title: Iran, Oman planning temporary corridor through Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran and Oman’s foreign ministers on Tuesday said they are setting up the framework of a temporary corridor for commercial vessels to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the key commercial waterway whose traffic has been stymied amid the U.S. war on Iran. Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi wrote on the social platform X that the…
articles.body:
Iran and Oman’s foreign ministers on Tuesday said they are setting up the framework of a temporary corridor for commercial vessels to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the key commercial waterway whose traffic has been stymied amid the U.S. war on Iran.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi wrote on the social platform X that the dialogue with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, about the new corridor was “constructive.”

“I am hopeful we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation. Future management of the Strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course, as per Article 5 of the Islamabad Memorandum,” al-Busaidi said, referring to the fifth point of the defunct interim peace deal signed by the U.S. and Iran in June.

His office stated that talks regarding the strait’s future would include an agreement on “a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services,” as well as the “importance of convening joint discussions with regional states bordering the waters of the Gulf.”

Araghchi separately wrote that during the conversation with Omani officials, “regional solutions were stressed.”

“Proposed framework for new corridor, joint mine-clearing and future management of Hormuz is case in point,” he added in an X post .

Traffic entering the Persian Gulf from the Gulf of Oman would pass through Iranian waters as outbound traffic would pass through waters belonging to either Iran or Oman, Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state TV, according to The Associated Press .

For a 30- to 60-day period, both countries will hold negotiations to “reach an understanding on a new permanent and sustainable route,” he said.

Iran has shut down much of the shipping that typically goes through the strait amid the nearly six-month conflict with the U.S., with the Trump administration seeking to control the passage with a naval blockade and President Trump posting a map claiming that the Strait of Hormuz is a U.S. territory . Iranian officials said they will reopen the strait after Trump withdraws the blockade.

It is unclear if the U.S. will accept the emerging deal. Trump previously threatened Oman over potentially striking a separate deal with Iran, warning the Persian Gulf country that “we’ll bomb the s‑‑‑ out of them” if Oman “gets in the way.”

Iran’s closure of the strait, lopping off the export of crude oil, caused gas and energy prices to soar in the months since the war began in February. The strait reopened following ceasefires and interim peace deals, including the memorandum of understanding signed by the U.S. and Iran in June, but they have all fizzled out.

Hostilities resumed, though tensions have lowered to a stalemate, with gas prices steadily rising since strike exchanges ceased. The national average for gas in the U.S. costs $4.10 per gallon, down 1 cent since last month but up nearly $1 since the average at this time last year, according to data from AAA .

articles.title: Quote of the day by Confucius: "The good man does not grieve that other people do not recognize his merits. His only anxiety is..."

articles.body: The desire to be recognised can quietly shape how people measure their success, confidence and self-worth. More than two thousand years ago, Chinese philosopher Confucius offered a different perspective, suggesting that people should be less concerned about whether others notice their achievements and more concerned about recognising the merits of those around them. In the Analects, Confucius wrote: “The good man does not grieve that other people do not recognize his merits. His only anxiety is lest he should fail to recognize theirs.” The quote presents humility as an important part of good character. Rather than constantly seeking praise or validation, Confucius encourages people to focus on recognising the abilities and contributions of others. His message remains relevant today, when recognition through careers, social media and public achievements can easily become a measure of personal worth.Quote of the day by Confucius“The good man does not grieve that other people do not recognize his merits. His only anxiety is lest he should fail to recognize theirs"Confucius's advice centres on a simple idea: do not make recognition from others the measure of your worth. The first part of the quote suggests that a person of good character should not become distressed simply because others fail to notice their achievements or abilities. Recognition can be satisfying, but constantly depending on it can make people vulnerable to disappointment and comparison. The second part of the quote turns the focus towards others. Confucius suggests that the greater concern should be whether we are failing to recognise the merits, abilities and accomplishments of the people around us.The message is not that achievements do not matter. Instead, it is about where a person's attention should be directed. Someone who is constantly asking whether others appreciate them may overlook the talents and contributions of those around them. Confucius presents humility as a form of strength, encouraging people to appreciate others without feeling that doing so diminishes their own achievements.Why people often seek recognitionRecognition can be a powerful motivator. People naturally want their hard work to be noticed, whether that comes through praise from a manager, appreciation from friends or acknowledgement from the wider public. Recognition can provide encouragement and help people feel that their efforts have meaning. However, relying too heavily on external approval can also create frustration when achievements go unnoticed or when someone else receives more attention.Confucius's words offer an alternative way of looking at achievement. Instead of constantly asking whether others have recognised our contributions, we can focus on doing meaningful work and maintaining good character regardless of how much attention it receives. This approach can also reduce the tendency to compare ourselves with others. A person who is comfortable with their own values and efforts may have less need to compete for recognition.The second half of the quote may be even more significant than the first. Confucius says the real concern should be “lest he should fail to recognize theirs”, placing responsibility on the individual to notice the qualities of others. Recognising someone else's talent does not diminish our own. In fact, acknowledging the contributions of colleagues, friends and mentors can strengthen relationships and create an environment in which people feel valued.This idea can be particularly important in workplaces and leadership. Good leaders need to recognise the people whose work contributes to a team's success rather than taking all the credit themselves. Similarly, people who openly appreciate the abilities of others can build stronger professional and personal relationships. Confucius's teaching therefore moves beyond personal humility and becomes a lesson in how we treat the people around us.Confucius and the lesson behind his wordsConfucius was a Chinese philosopher and teacher whose ideas about ethics, education, relationships and personal conduct profoundly influenced Chinese thought and wider East Asian culture. His teachings were recorded by his students and later followers in the Analects, a collection of conversations and observations about how people should live and conduct themselves. The quote about recognition appears in the Analects as part of Confucius's broader emphasis on self-improvement and moral character.For Confucius, becoming a better person involved continuous self-examination. Rather than concentrating exclusively on how others judged us, his teachings encouraged people to examine their own behaviour and responsibilities. The quote reflects that wider philosophy by shifting attention away from receiving praise and towards recognising virtue in others.The timeless lessonConfucius's words ultimately offer a lesson about humility, recognition and self-worth. Being overlooked can be frustrating, particularly when someone has worked hard or achieved something meaningful, but constant concern about receiving credit can distract from the achievement itself. At the same time, failing to recognise the talents and efforts of others can prevent us from learning from them and appreciating what they contribute.The quote encourages a healthier balance. We can take pride in our own work without requiring constant approval, while remaining generous enough to recognise excellence in others. In a world where recognition is often measured through promotions, awards, followers and public praise, Confucius's message remains strikingly relevant: our character may be revealed not by how desperately we seek recognition, but by how willingly we recognise the worth of others.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Deadly flash floods in Nepal leave hundreds missing, including tourists from US
articles.summary: Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries such as India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia, were among those reported missing.
articles.body:
UDIN DHUNGA, Nepal (AP) — Massive flash floods in Nepal on Wednesday killed at least 22 people and left hundreds of tourists, workers and others missing while causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries such as India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia, were reported missing.

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9 a.m. local time Wednesday, destroying several villages, roads and hydropower projects, officials said.

“We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.

Dozens of multistoried buildings, trucks and vans were buried under vast quantities of mud in the district of Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected areas. Officials warned residents in several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli, and Narayani rivers.

Nepal tourism board officials said most of the missing were likely tourists from India and the Indian diaspora on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in the Chinese autonomous region of Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.

South Korean government officials said their citizens working on building a hydropower plant in Nepal were among those reported missing.

Malaysia’s Foreign Ministry also said its embassy in Kathmandu has received reports from travel agencies that they had lost contact with 11 Malaysians believed to be in the Rasuwa district, which was hit hard by the floods.

Meanwhile, Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Authorities didn’t announce any numbers of dead or injured.

Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up the efforts for people missing after the mudslide, state news agency Xinhua reported. Xi also called for residents at risk to be evacuated from any area on the Chinese side.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered help. “India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts,” Modi said in a social media post.

The same regions affected by Wednesday’s disaster saw flash floods similar to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighboring Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged at the time.

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday’s flash flood.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said.

“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in fourteen months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.

“In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation,” he added.

The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal and several nearby countries , including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because it is warming faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research shows that extreme weather events, including heat waves and rains, and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region.

Researchers in Kathmandu found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

Associated Press writer Hyung-jin Kim in Seoul, South Korea, and Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, contributed to this report.

articles.title: Inquest begins into death of Jason Arday
articles.summary: Dr Julian Morris Morris said he had "reason to suspect that Professor Arday died an unnatural death".
articles.body:
An inquest has begun into the death of Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row.

He was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, days after resigning from his post.

His appointment as Cambridge's youngest ever black professor at the age of 37 in 2023 was hailed at the time as a progressive moment.

Senior coroner Dr Julian Morris said on Wednesday: "The various reports have given me reason to suspect that Professor Arday died an unnatural death 12 days ago."

He told London Inner South Coroner's Court: "It therefore follows that I must open an investigation."

The Metropolitan Police said at the time that Arday's death was being treated as unexpected and was "not believed to be suspicious".

Arday was found "unresponsive" by family members at his home in Battersea, the inquest heard on Wednesday. Despite resuscitation efforts he was pronounced dead, the inquest was told.

The 41-year-old had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

He said controversy about his work had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

The claims emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. Such scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics, he said.

After his death, his family issued a statement saying they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former Cambridge professor before his death.

Arday's memoir is due to be published in the UK on Thursday. The publisher, Simon & Schuster, announced on Monday that the book will be released as planned, with his family saying: "It is only right that we honour his wishes."

articles.title: Don’t let China rescue Cuba
articles.summary: The Chinese in Cuba have maintained a “persistent intelligence-gathering presence.”
articles.body:
On Aug. 6, the U.S. State Department sanctioned Cuba’s senior military representative in China, Waldo Perez Cortes. Cortes was among six Cuban nationals and five entities added to the Treasury Department’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List. According to the State Department, Cortes aided “the procurement of military-related equipment from China to Cuba.”

The action looks merely symbolic, because Cortes and the other sanctioned parties are unlikely to have assets or banking relationships in the U.S. But American pressure against the regime is real. Cuba’s 10 million residents have experienced electricity blackouts in part because the island is under an almost airtight American energy blockade.

The U.S. has interdicted energy shipments to the island since late January , cut off the flow of Venezuelan oil after the early January capture of Nicolas Maduro and his wife and threatened sanctions on countries supplying fuel to the Cuban regime.

Yet although American actions have had a severe effect, they have not been the root cause of the island’s electricity interruptions. The blackouts, after all, have been occurring since 2024 . Fuel imports and domestic oil production have been in a long-term decline. The regime once led by Fidel Castro had long ago run Cuba into the ground.

The Trump administration has evidently sensed an opportunity. Led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Washington has done everything short of an invasion to bring down the regime now headed by Communist Party First Secretary Miguel Diaz-Canel.

In July, the State Department issued a report titled “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism.” The capital of communism this century is China — not Cuba. But the report is correct when it states that Cuba is where “the ambitions of Moscow, Beijing, and Tehran converge,” and in pointing out that the island is a “force multiplier” for an “anti-American coalition.”

As a part of that coalition, the Chinese in Cuba have maintained a “persistent intelligence-gathering presence.” The State Department report notes that Beijing “actively runs three of Cuba’s 18 known” signals intelligence locations.

In 2024, the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified four such locations. There is, most prominently, the Lourdes facility just west of Havana near Bejucal, once the Soviet Union’s largest listening station outside its borders. The Chinese are thought to have taken over the facility just after the fall of the Soviet Union. There is also another one from the Soviet era, Calabazar . One, Wajay, appears to have been built after the fall of the Soviet Union. There is also a new station, El Salao .

Some believe China’s intelligence presence on the island began with the visit of China’s Defense Minister General, Chi Haotian, in 1999, but R. Evan Ellis of the U.S. Army War College told me that the Chinese may have been operating listening posts in Cuba since 1993. The intelligence relationship between Beijing and Havana, therefore, is both deep and longstanding.

Moreover, the threat is great. In its report , the State Department said it “poses an acute risk to U.S. military operational security,” and Cuba is among China’s “most critical foreign listening posts.”

“After being surprised by Venezuela, China is attentive to U.S. military action in Cuba but will probably hold on to its strategically valuable electronics and signals intelligence collection facilities in Cuba until the day they are kicked out,” Ellis told me earlier this month.

So how does the U.S. remove the Chinese from Cuba?

“We can do to the Chinese in Cuba what they do to us in the South China Sea: take actions just below the threshold of war,” Blaine Holt, a retired U.S. Air Force general, told me. “Create pain. Stick them with a million pins.”

“We should take actions that cut off the life support for China’s personnel in Cuba, such as restricting flights in and out of the island,” said Holt, who once served as deputy U.S. military advisor to NATO. “Let’s see if the Chinese are happy staying there without, for instance, Chinese food. The Chinese should not complain. After all, they tell us they’re not doing anything on the island, so our response should be, ‘What’s it to you?'”

And that brings us back to energy. China has been helping Cuba generate electricity with solar power from its panels, especially since 2024. There are already solar parks that supply about 10 percent of the country’s demand for electricity, up from 3 percent in 2025. As the Wall Street Journal put it , Chinese-provided solar power is “offering an unlikely bright spot for a power grid plagued by fuel shortages, crumbling infrastructure and near-daily blackouts.”

So, in addition to interdicting Chinese food, the U.S. needs to stop the Chinese from bringing in solar panels.

articles.title: Israel extends campaign against UNRWA to advance West Bank annexation
articles.summary: Raid on UNRWA centre exposes Israel’s strategic push to erase refugee rights, seal West Bank annexation, analysts say.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have raided the Qalandiya Training Centre, operated by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in occupied East Jerusalem in what officials and analysts describe as a pivotal step towards dismantling international refugee protections and consolidating control over the occupied West Bank.

Tuesday’s storming of the UNRWA facility, led by far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, was justified by Israeli authorities under October 2024 legislation banning the UN agency, prompting sharp condemnation from Qatar, which warned of systematic efforts to strip millions of Palestinians of essential services.

Israeli affairs expert Adel Shadid identified broader territorial ambitions behind the raid, carried out on the boundary line between East Jerusalem and the West Bank. He told Al Jazeera the assault serves a larger geopolitical scheme involving a historic airport close to the training centre.

“The institute is directly adjacent to the historic Qalandiya Airport, which was built more than 106 years ago,” Shadid said.

“The occupation aims to gain complete control over the airport adjacent to the institute to establish a massive settlement comprising over 9,000 settlement units in addition to a Jewish heritage centre and to erase the historical and geographical Jordanian landmarks of the airport,” he explained.

“By controlling these two areas and annexing them to the occupation municipality, the pillars of the ‘Greater Jerusalem’ project are completed. This project alone will carve out between 12 to 13 percent of the total area of the West Bank,” he added.

Shadid noted that this expansion would allow the municipality to control an area exceeding 800sq km (310sq miles), essentially destroying Palestinian continuity.

“The ultimate goal of the occupation exceeds preventing the establishment of a future Palestinian state. Rather, it aims explicitly to prevent the establishment of any independent Palestinian entity or presence on this land,” he said.

Echoing this assessment, retired Lebanese Brigadier General and military analyst Elias Hanna pointed to Israel’s tactical encirclement of urban Palestinian hubs.

“The importance of Qalandiya is linked to the broader settlement project in the West Bank, which is based on creating settlement blocs aiming to control geographical continuity between Palestinian areas and isolate them from each other,” Hanna told Al Jazeera.

“The control over the area can affect the movement and connection between the two cities,” he added, referring to Jerusalem and Ramallah.

Detailing the immediate impact on UNRWA’s institutional mandate, the agency’s media adviser Adnan Abu Hasna outlined the unprecedented nature of the takeover.

“UNRWA was not informed [in advance] of any action by the Israeli government against the UNRWA institute and complex in Qalandiya,” Abu Hasna told Al Jazeera.

“This measure is unprecedented as the UN flag is lowered and this headquarters is taken over in this unusual manner, and it represents a dangerous escalation against international humanitarian law, against UN laws and against the mandate granted to UNRWA by the UN General Assembly,” he said.

Abu Hasna underscored how the raid violated historic bilateral frameworks that long governed UN operations.

“There is an agreement signed between UNRWA and Israel on June 14, 1967, providing for facilitating UNRWA’s operations and protecting its facilities and its employees and headquarters enjoying immunity and privileges, but unfortunately, all of this has ended now under the weight of escalating Israeli measures,” he said.

The agency operates schools and provides healthcare, social services and microfinancing for Palestinians. Compounding the Israeli raids, destructions of its compounds and offices, and restrictions on its operations, the agency is also facing a financial crisis. Abu Hasna cited major political defunding campaigns, particularly by the United States.

“We have a large deficit, especially after the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers cut $360m, which constitutes about 30 percent of UNRWA’s annual budget,” he noted.

Regarding the operational dynamics on the ground, Israeli affairs specialist Anas Abu Arqoub highlighted the deepening alignment between state forces and armed settlers.

“It is a division of roles accompanied by a state of complete integration,” Abu Arqoub told Al Jazeera.

“The settler phenomenon … [is] in fact armed organisations with a clear leadership hierarchy, a system of regular and reserve fighters called upon when needed, and they possess a military combat doctrine,” he explained.

“A large part of them are elements from within the Israeli army, armed with its weapons, and undergo joint military training,” he added.

Abu Arqoub said Israeli research institutions, such as the Institute for National Security Studies, have recognised the severe implications of this convergence.

“The Institute for National Security Studies recently pointed out that this military force of settlers has become capable, under the cover of ‘loss of control’, of executing complete ethnic cleansing in the West Bank,” he observed.

Examining the international impunity enabling these actions, Birzeit University political science Professor Ghassan Khatib emphasised Washington’s decisive role.

“The weakness of the United Nations position is one of the two main factors driving Israel to persist and increasingly rebel against international laws and violate the rights of the Palestinian people,” Khatib told Al Jazeera.

“The first and most important factor is the American position, the actual sponsor of this Israeli rebellion,” he stressed, pointing out a “direct correlation between the rising pace of Israeli violations and the reascent of [President Donald] Trump to the leadership of the United States about two years ago”.

“These settler militias have become an integral part of the occupation system, and the danger will inevitably escalate,” Khatib added.

From the local community’s perspective, Mohammed Saeed – public relations director for the popular committee of the Qalandiya refugee camp, which Israeli forces also raided on Tuesday – framed the raid as both diplomatic defiance and domestic political posturing.

The Israeli incursion, he said, was a clear message of defiance stating: ‘We are the owners of the land, and we decide its fate,'” Saeed told Al Jazeera on Tuesday.

articles.title: Trump: If Ayatollah is dead, Iran ‘putting on a good show’
articles.summary: President Trump said Wednesday he does not believe Iran’s supreme leader is dead after a report suggested he could be deceased or brain-dead. “He was very seriously wounded, but I don’t think he’s dead,” Trump said in an interview with conservative commentator Glenn Beck. “And if he is, they’re putting on a pretty good show…
articles.body:
President Trump said Wednesday he does not believe Iran’s supreme leader is dead after a report suggested he could be deceased or brain-dead.

“He was very seriously wounded, but I don’t think he’s dead,” Trump said in an interview with conservative commentator Glenn Beck.

“And if he is, they’re putting on a pretty good show because they talk about going back to talk to him all the time to get a final blessing on things,” he added.

A Tuesday report from The Atlantic cited sources in Tehran speculating that Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei was either dead or brain-dead. Others believed he was still alive.

Khamenei, the son of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was selected to be Iran’s new leader after his father was killed during Operation Epic Fury in February.

But the younger Khamenei has not been seen in public or in photographs since. It was reported that he was badly wounded in the strikes that killed his father.

“He was very seriously wounded,” Trump said. “The left side of his body, the arm, the leg, the whole thing.”

The president went on to say that the Iranians are “not the most honorable group” to deal with, as he seeks to end a war that has now dragged on for nearly six months.

Direct talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled. Iran and Oman have continued to hold discussions on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran insists the U.S. must lift its naval blockade on the strait.

Trump told Beck that the strait is “functioning.”

“We take a lot of ships through the strait now. We’re taking them in,” he said. “The mines are gone.”

He said “every once in a while” a drone or rocket will be shot, “but it is a very functioning strait.”

Shipping trackers have reported an uptick in oil coming out of the waterway in recent weeks, but traffic remains far below prewar levels.

articles.title: State Department warns Americans of travel to Mexicali

The advisory, issued by the U.S. Embassy in Mexico, noted the U.S. government was suspending its consular activities in the border city on Tuesday. The Hill has reached out to the State Department for clarification on whether…
articles.body:
The State Department on Monday issued a travel advisory for Americans visiting the northern Mexican city of Mexicali.

The advisory , issued by the U.S. Embassy in Mexico, noted the U.S. government was suspending its consular activities in the border city on Tuesday. The Hill has reached out to the State Department for clarification on whether the suspension is still in effect.

The advisory did not give a specific reason for the status change beyond “threat information,” but instructed U.S. citizens to avoid government buildings in Mexicali, seek shelter in the event of an incident and follow instructions from Mexican law enforcement.

More than 1 million people lived in Mexicali as of 2020, according to the Mexican government . The city is a short drive from the California border city of Calexico.

Mexican Secretary of Security and Citizen Protection wrote Thursday on social media that Mexican authorities, with assistance from officials in Mexicali, carried out an operation at a property linked to the “Los Rusos” criminal group.

“During the operation, 120 kilos of fentanyl pills were seized, equivalent to more than 4 million doses, in addition to a firearm and vehicles,” added Garcia Harfuch, who noted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration provided Mexican authorities with information ahead of the raid.

U.S. Northern Command on Tuesday commended the Mexican government’s “success” against Los Rusos, writing on social media the country’s “whole-of-government commitment to countering cartels is reducing illicit trafficking at the Southern Border.”

The Security Cabinet of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Tuesday authorities have not identified anything to confirm a risk to the population.

“As a preventative measure, federal, state and municipal authorities are reinforcing patrol and surveillance actions at strategic points in Mexicali,” the cabinet added in a statement .

articles.title: Baltimore mayor backs ballot measure creating taxpayer-funded 'Baby Fund' for newborn families
articles.summary: Brandon Scott backs the Baltimore Baby Fund ballot measure that could fund direct cash payments to parents of newborns through a dedicated property tax.
articles.body: Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott is backing a ballot measure to establish a municipal fund that could provide direct cash payments, subsidies, or supplies to parents of newborns. Recently, Scott and the campaign behind the Baltimore Baby Fund (BBF) issued a joint statement outlining their collaboration to build public support for the measure ahead of the election. "Mayor Scott and the Baltimore Baby Fund campaign look forward to working together in the months ahead to earn voters’ support and, if the initiative passes, outline a program that gives Baltimore’s babies and families the strongest possible start," the BBF campaign posted on Instagram. ALBUQUERQUE USES WEED TAX TO FUND 'NO-STRINGS-ATTACHED' GUARANTEED INCOME, SPARKING POLICY DEBATE The announcement comes after organizers submitted more than the 10,000 signatures required to qualify for the ballot. The initiative officially secured a spot on the November ballot following structural revisions. Voters will decide whether to amend the city charter to establish a dedicated, permanent line item in the municipal budget for the fund. If approved, the measure would require the city to allocate 3 cents per $100 of assessed property value into the fund. The City Council would retain authority over the specific disbursement rules and eligibility criteria through future enabling legislation. CHICAGO SUBURB EXPANDS CASH HANDOUTS AS RACE-BASED REPARATIONS PROGRAM FACES MAJOR LEGAL BATTLE "Mayor Scott has always been supportive of the policy ideas driving the Baltimore Baby Fund campaign, and, now with the necessary adjustments made in the 2026 version, is eager to move it forward," the BBF statement read. The proposed fund is modeled after Rx Kids, a high-profile cash assistance program for prenatal and infant care launched in Flint, Michigan. Co-founded by pediatrician Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha and University of Michigan professor Luke Shaefer following the Flint water crisis, Rx Kids has expanded to dozens of communities across Michigan, providing eligible expectant mothers with $1,500 during pregnancy and $500 per month for six to 12 months after a child's birth, depending on location. MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS The initiative aligns with broader efforts by Mayors for a Guaranteed Income, a coalition of over 150 U.S. mayors advocating for direct cash distributions to address cost-of-living concerns. The coalition has supported more than 100 pilot programs across the country since 2018, including a program in Cook County, Illinois, which subsequently approved local funding to make its guaranteed income initiative permanent. Scott, National Co-Chair of Mayors for Guaranteed Income, previously oversaw a localized direct-cash pilot in Baltimore. Operating from August 2022 to July 2024, the Baltimore Young Families Success Fund provided unconditional payments to low-income parents and guardians aged 18 to 24 earning at or below 300% of the federal poverty level. "During the meeting, Mayor Scott, National Co-Chair of Mayors for Guaranteed Income, shared that he views the fund as a natural evolution of his Administration’s guaranteed income pilot, which provided cash assistance to young parents. Participants in the pilot missed less work, were less likely to be food insecure, and had less stress," the BBF statement noted. It continued, "They used the money to continue their educations, pay down debt, save for emergencies, and invest in their children. Mayor Scott has always been supportive of the policy ideas driving the Baltimore Baby Fund campaign, and, now with the necessary adjustments made in the 2026 version, is eager to move it forward." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Neither the Scott administration nor representatives for the BBF campaign responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

articles.summary: President Trump referred to CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s trip to Russia this week as “semi-routine” after the Kremlin confirmed Ratcliffe was in the country to meet intelligence officials. “I hate to disappoint people,” Trump told conservative talks show host Glenn Beck on Wednesday. “John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA,…
articles.body:
President Trump referred to CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s trip to Russia this week as “semi-routine” after the Kremlin confirmed Ratcliffe was in the country to meet intelligence officials.

“I hate to disappoint people,” Trump told conservative talks show host Glenn Beck on Wednesday.

“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things you said,” he continued, referring to Beck noting there is speculation that Ratcliffe’s visit could test NATO resolve.

“Now something may come out, you know, out of it,” he said. “Frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point,” he said, referring to Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with his Russian intelligence counterparts in Moscow this week, but did not meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Of course, President Putin is immediately informed of everything,” Peskov said, according to The Associated Press.

The visit is Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia since being confirmed as the CIA director in 2025.

The Trump administration asked Ukrainian officials last week not to strike Moscow, St. Petersburg and northern regions of the country with its long-range drones and missiles Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday because the U.S. was sending a senior official to Moscow, Financial Times reported .

articles.title: Senate Democrats press Netanyahu on ‘surge’ in West Bank violence
articles.summary: A majority of Senate Democrats have signed a Wednesday letter urging Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to address the “surge” in violence in the West Bank amid tensions from the Gaza war. The conflict is driven in part by Israeli settlers who are forcefully laying claim to land where Palestinians reside. “Incidents of fatal violence…
articles.body:
A majority of Senate Democrats have signed a Wednesday letter urging Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to address the “surge” in violence in the West Bank amid tensions from the Gaza war.

The conflict is driven in part by Israeli settlers who are forcefully laying claim to land where Palestinians reside.

“Incidents of fatal violence by settlers have reportedly already surpassed 2025 levels and continue to increase. The last few weeks alone saw a significant surge in violence on both sides, resulting in a large-scale response by Israeli security forces, mass arrests of Palestinians, and reported attacks by settlers on mosques,” the lawmakers, led by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), wrote in the letter.

“We urge you to take measures to prevent and intercede in this violence, establish a credible mechanism to investigate violations of law, and to make clear that the Government of Israel will not tolerate violence by its people, just as it does not tolerate violence against its people,” they added.

The Israeli Embassy did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Israeli settler attacks have risen by roughly 63 percent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, with hundreds of violent incidents recorded, as reported by the United Nation Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

There have been 660 settler attacks during the first six months of the year, compared with the 405 attacks during the same period in 2025.

The escalation has forced the displacement of thousands of Palestinians from rural communities and isolated villages in response to direct threats, property destruction and restricted access to basic resources like water and electricity.

Americans residing in the West Bank have been impacted by the conditions. American Naim Abu Siyam, 19, was shot and killed by Israeli settlers in February inside the village of Mukhmas, while Sayfollah Musallet, 20, of Tampa, Fla., was beaten to death by settlers in July of last year for attempting to protect his family’s farmland.

Democratic senators are urging Netanyahu to intervene.

“We write particularly on behalf of American citizens who have been killed or threatened in such violence. Many of us have heard first-hand from their families and other constituents who have themselves been threatened without cause by settlers,” the senators wrote.

“We have engaged the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem and your embassy in Washington to ensure their protection and appreciate measures taken on their behalf, but a more significant response from your government is clearly needed. We ask for your personal and direct engagement and intervention in order to protect our constituents and their families,” they added.

The only two senators who did not sign on to the letter were Democratic Sens. John Fetterman (Pa.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.).

articles.title: Meet Ashka Shah, the 17-year-old New York student who studied how a cancer-driving protein enters the cell nucleus and found a way to block its harmful signalling while preserving its normal function
articles.summary: US News: A 17-year-old student from New York has developed a targeted method to stop cancer cells from growing, earning national recognition for tackling one o.
articles.body: A 17-year-old student from New York has developed a targeted method to stop cancer cells from growing, earning national recognition for tackling one of the biggest challenges in cancer research. Ashka Shah, a senior at Jericho High School on Long Island, developed a method that blocks the harmful activity of a key cancer-driving protein without stopping its important functions in healthy cells. Her research earned her a place as a finalist in the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search, one of the oldest and most prestigious science and maths competitions for American high school students. The project focuses on the Wnt signalling pathway, an important biological system that controls normal cell growth, stem cell maintenance and tissue repair. When mutations occur, a key protein in this pathway, beta-catenin, can build up in large amounts and move into the cell nucleus. There, it activates genes that help aggressive tumours grow, especially in liver and colorectal cancers.Separating cancer growth from healthy functionScientists have struggled to target beta-catenin because the protein has two very different roles in the body. Outside the nucleus, beta-catenin helps form important structures that hold healthy cells together. Completely blocking the protein can therefore cause serious toxicity and damage healthy tissues. Shah focused instead on how mutant beta-catenin gets into the nucleus and causes harm. According to her project profile published by the Society for Science, Shah found that a helper protein called Gid8 helps mutant beta-catenin enter the nucleus, where it switches on genes linked to cancer growth. Using fruit fly models, cultured human liver cancer cells and molecular binding experiments, Shah identified a small section of the beta-catenin protein that could interfere with this process. By introducing the targeted peptide, she was able to block the Gid8-assisted transport system. This stopped the mutant beta-catenin from reaching the nucleus and driving uncontrolled cell growth, while allowing the protein to continue performing its important structural role in healthy tissue. Her project, formally titled "Selective Dual Inhibition of beta-Catenin in Wnt-Driven Cancers via Gid8-Assisted Translocation and a Precision Peptide-Based Gene Therapy," presents a possible new approach to precision cancer treatment.National recognition for her researchShah was selected as one of 40 national finalists from 2,612 applicants across the United States. It was the largest group of applicants to the competition since 1967. The Society for Science selects finalists based on the originality of their research, scientific quality and leadership. According to official competition records, each of the 40 finalists receives at least 25,000 dollars, while the top awards can reach 250,000 dollars. The final judging takes place in Washington, D.C. Shah's work in molecular biology is only one part of her wider academic and community involvement. She is president of Jericho High School's Medical Minds Club, captain of the school's varsity fencing team and involved in local community service projects.A possible path towards precision cancer treatmentFinding treatments that can block cancer-related activity without damaging healthy cells remains a major goal in cancer research. Many current treatments affect both cancerous and healthy cells, which can lead to serious side effects. Shah's research takes a more targeted approach by focusing on the Gid8 mechanism that helps move beta-catenin into the nucleus. By blocking this specific interaction, her work suggests that the cancer-driving activity of beta-catenin could potentially be stopped while leaving its normal functions in healthy cells untouched. The research presented to the Society for Science points towards the possibility of using peptide-based gene therapies to target this transport process. Such an approach could eventually provide a more precise option than treatments that affect healthy organs along with cancer cells.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Montana man reportedly asked to leave parents’ home before opening fire
articles.summary: A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, as they gathered for dinner at a Montana home, weeks after his parents asked him to move out, a family member said.
articles.body: A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, as they gathered for dinner at a Montana home, weeks after his parents asked him to move out, a family member said. Brad Ireland, whose former wife and two children were among the dead, identified the shooter as 44-year-old Alan Smith. Smith’s parents, who were also killed, had asked him to move out, but he returned on Sunday and opened fire just outside of Billings, Ireland said. The victims represented four generations of the blended family, ranging from a great-grandmother in her 90s who used a wheelchair to a 7-year-old girl, according to Jennifer Mercer, a neighbor and family friend who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses, and was authorized to release these details. Gunshots followed by an inferno Police responded to the home on Sunday evening and heard gunshots coming from out back, just before the house was completely engulfed in flames. Investigators confirmed Tuesday there were eight victims, including four children, and that the suspect had suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound and later died. The investigation has been complicated by concerns about the structural integrity of the house after the fire burned it to its foundation, said Jeff Stovall, a spokesperson for the Billings Police Department. Firefighters fought the blaze until around 1 a.m. Monday, according to Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel. The home is in a subdivision outside of city limits that’s not required to have fire hydrants. Efforts to fight the fire were delayed until the site was secure, allowing the blaze to tear through the home. 12-year-old calls 911 Among those killed were Ireland’s ex-wife, Megan Ghekiere, and their two children, Owen Ireland, 13, and Chloe Ireland, 7. Also killed were Ghekiere’s two stepchildren with her current husband: Landon Ghekiere, 15, and Charlotte Ghekiere, 12. “The one thing we do know is that Charlotte was the hero,” Mercer said. “Charlotte called 911 and she tried to save her family. And that’s something the family does want out there.” She described the family as “very loving and close,” and said the children all got along and that their parents remained amicable even after divorcing. “I feel like our entire community is devastated, even people that never knew any of them,” Mercer said. The family relocated from Seattle The Smith family was originally from the Seattle area. Ireland said that after he and Megan Ghekiere divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children. That’s where she met the man who would become her second husband, Adam Ghekiere, who was working and not at the home when the shooting occurred. Her parents, Dana and Barb Smith, soon followed, buying a house in Billings near their daughter’s home. Evelyn Smith, Dana’s elderly mother, lived in a nearby retirement community, Ireland said. “They were nice,” neighbor Donna Heisler, 67, told NBC News on Tuesday. “I talked to Barbara the wife at a couple of garage sales.” Heisler said her neighbors appeared to enjoy their privacy. “They kind of kept to themselves. Really weren’t a very outgoing couple,” Heisler said. “They weren’t the socialites on the block so you’d see them once in a while but they weren’t overly outgoing.” She added: “And coming from a bigger city maybe more the way they preferred to have it.” Alan Smith moved in with his parents in Montana and stayed with them for years before being asked to move out a couple weeks ago, Ireland said. He unexpectedly returned to the home on Sunday evening, where the Smiths had gathered for a weekly family dinner. Alan Smith killed his grandmother, his parents, his younger sister and the four children before setting the house on fire, Ireland said. He tried to flee before being confronted by law enforcement, he said. Suspect was a ‘hermit,’ relative says “There were many red flags and many people spoke out,” said Ireland, who lives in Arizona. “No one listened.” Alan Smith was a “hermit” who spent most of his days in his room on his computer, Ireland said. “No one knew what he did in there 24/7,” he said. Alan Smith had attended Eastern Washington University but had been unable to find or hold a job. A search of criminal records in Montana and Washington found no record Alan Smith had ever been arrested or charged with a crime. Ireland said that to his knowledge Alan Smith had never been violent, though he could be verbally abusive. Friends of the victims have set up two GoFundMe accounts to raise money on behalf of Adam Ghekiere and his ex-wife, Erica Schneider. Husband races back to house Adam Ghekiere, who works at the airport in Billings, told the AP that he heard over a dispatch radio about an active shooting. After calling each member of his family, he raced across town to the Smith home. When he got there, the house was ablaze, and two hours later, he learned his wife and children had been killed. His children weren’t supposed to be there because family dinner was usually on Friday, he said. “I don’t think he expected my kids to be there,” Ghekiere said, referring to his brother-in-law. “Monster isn’t even enough to describe what he did.” Ghekiere said police confirmed his daughter, Charlotte, was the one who dialed 911 from inside the house. “I keep hearing her quote to me every time I would say ‘I love you’ and she would say ‘I love you more,’” he said.
